clue.text: Ship of comparatively fit women must come first

indicators.note: the clue says the women letter has to lead, so it is placed ahead of the fitness word

parts.note: hale means fit and healthy, so its comparative form is haler

explanation.surface: A ladies' fitness boast: the healthier crew of women must take priority aboard a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A whaling vessel is a type of ship, so the word names a ship as well as its crewman.

clue.text: Despicable criminal in house

indicators.note: criminal suggests something bent out of true, so the letters of in and house are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wicked crook lurking inside a home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' looks like a noun but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something heinous is utterly wicked and odious, hence deserving contempt.

clue.text: Cash obtained from clubs in draw

indicators.note: in places the card suit letter within the word for draw

parts.note: to lure is to draw or attract
C is the abbreviation for clubs in cards

explanation.surface: Money won at the clubs in a lottery draw.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucre is a somewhat disparaging word for money, as in filthy lucre.

clue.text: What visitors do sound familiar?

definitions.meaning: callers at a house press the doorbell to announce themselves
the idiom for something seeming vaguely known or recalled

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally describes pressing a doorbell and idiomatically means to stir a memory.

clue.text: Key employed by Rolling Stones right for crooner?

indicators.note: something employed by a group is taken into it, so the key letter sits inside the other letters
rolling suggests tumbling around, so the letters of Stones plus R are rearranged

parts.note: G is a musical key

explanation.surface: Which key do the Rolling Stones use, and is the right one fit for a crooner?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolling' shuffles STONES plus R into SONSTER; 'employed by' puts the key G inside it. The question mark flags that a crooner is just one example of a singer.
explanation.definitionFit: A crooner is one kind of singer, and the word names any singer of songs, so it fits by example.

clue.text: By-product of political bias being absent?

parts.note: spin is the slanted presentation of news by politicians
off means away or absent, as in a day off

explanation.surface: A side effect of politics without spin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link word; the question mark admits the playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A secondary product or benefit derived from a main one is a by-product.

clue.text: Demands nothing except energy, dedication and stamina at first

indicators.note: at first means the opening letter of each of the five words is taken in turn

explanation.surface: A coach's list of demands: nothing but energy, dedication and stamina.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is a link; 'except' is easily skipped but gives the second E.
explanation.definitionFit: Needs as a noun are requirements, things demanded, matching demands in the plural.

clue.text: Perhaps Mediterranean ranchers losing millions could become sailors

parts.note: the Mediterranean is an example of a sea, the 'perhaps' marking an example

indicators.note: losing means giving up, so the letter for millions is taken out

parts.note: ranchers are farmers

explanation.surface: Mediterranean ranchers going broke might take to the sea as sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could become' is link material.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who travel by sea, especially regularly as crew, are mariners, which is what sailors are.

clue.text: Look at dance after a bit of needle

indicators.note: after puts the dance second, following the needle part

parts.note: the eye is the hole in a needle, a part of it
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Someone eyes up a dance after a quick injection.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball something is slang for staring at it or inspecting it closely.

clue.text: Self-centred new Conservative team enveloped by anger

indicators.note: being enveloped means being wrapped round, so the outer word surrounds the run of pieces

parts.note: irate means full of anger; the clue word stands for the angry state
a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: A political grumble: a self-serving new Tory team surrounded by public fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anger' must be read loosely as the adjective for angry; the container splits it after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone self-centred gives no thought to other people, which is exactly a thoughtless, uncaring person.

clue.text: Piece of music on-line monitor cut short?

indicators.note: cutting something short removes its tail, so the final letter goes

parts.note: someone who polices an internet forum is its moderator

explanation.surface: A web forum's watchdog is curtailed, and somehow a bit of music results.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the stretch of calling a forum official's title, shortened, a musical piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A movement marked to be played at moderate speed is often titled by that tempo marking, so it names a piece.

clue.text: Camp needing a convict on the way?

indicators.note: in an across answer one piece written on another follows it, so the street comes before the rest

parts.note: ST is short for street, a way
LAG is slang for a convict, as in old lag

explanation.surface: A prison camp that needs an inmate travelling on the road to it.
explanation.walkthrough: A stalag was a German prisoner-of-war camp; 'old lag' is British slang for a long-serving convict.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalag was a German prisoner-of-war camp in the Second World War, a specific kind of camp.

clue.text: Grounds given by judge dismissing firm regularly

indicators.note: to dismiss is to send away, so the chosen letters are taken out of the longer word

parts.note: to judge an amount is to estimate it

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter of firm is picked, here the second and fourth

explanation.surface: A legal scene: grounds a judge offers for regularly throwing out a company's case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' picks I and M, the even letters of firm, and 'dismissing' removes them from ESTIMATE.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is a large area of land around a country house, that is, its grounds.

clue.text: Burden that golfer with a hole in one might register?

definitions.meaning: a heavy weight one is stuck with, after the bird in Coleridge's Ancient Mariner

definitions.text: that golfer with a hole in one might register?
definitions.meaning: a hole in one on a par-four is three under par, the rarest golf score

explanation.definitionFit: The seabird stands for a burden from Coleridge's poem, and also names a score three under par in golf.

clue.text: Somehow rely on social behaviour, for once

indicators.note: in an across answer one piece written on another follows it, so the rearranged letters come second

parts.note: form is accepted social conduct, as in good form or bad form

indicators.note: somehow means in some unexplained way, so the letters of rely are rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice to trust in good manners, just this once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link word. 'Good form' is British for correct behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Once, meaning at some earlier time, is a synonym for in the past or previously.

clue.text: Case of rare trouble during disturbed rest for shopkeepers

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, so the first and last letters of rare are taken
during means within the span of, so the trouble sits inside the rearranged letters
disturbed means upset or shaken about, so the letters of rest are rearranged

parts.note: to ail is to trouble, as in what ails you

explanation.surface: A rare spot of bother during a restless night for shop owners.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram makes TERS, and the trouble goes in after its T.
explanation.definitionFit: Retailers sell goods to the public from shops, so they are shopkeepers.

clue.text: Story about international doctor and southern dishes

indicators.note: about means round, so the story surrounds the two short pieces

parts.note: a tale is a story
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: A tale of a globetrotting physician and the cuisine of the South.
explanation.walkthrough: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is the British doctor's degree; 'doctor' here is not DR.
explanation.definitionFit: Timbales are moulded savoury dishes, named after the drum-shaped moulds they are cooked in.

clue.text: Popular drink with endless kids is lacking taste

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a sip is a small drink

indicators.note: endless means with both ends removed, leaving only the middle of kids

explanation.surface: A popular soft drink for children turns out bland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Insipid food or drink has little flavour, so it is bland and without savour.

clue.text: Spurs going on-line?

parts.note: spurs here are short branch tracks off a railway line, not riders' spurs or the football club joining the internet

explanation.surface: Tottenham Hotspurs, nicknamed Spurs, launching themselves on the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: Spurs is a London football club's nickname; railway spurs are short branches off the main line.
explanation.definitionFit: Short tracks branching off a main railway line, where trains are parked, are railway spurs.

clue.text: Experiences discrimination, say, initially

parts.note: taste is discernment, the ability to discriminate between good and bad

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter of say is used

explanation.surface: Someone describes facing prejudice, at least at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Experiences discrimination' reads as a phrase about prejudice; here discrimination means refined judgement.
explanation.definitionFit: To taste something is to undergo it briefly, as in tasting freedom, so the verb matches experiences.

clue.text: Material like this gives bands a chance to stretch out and play?

definitions.text: Material like this gives bands a chance to stretch out and play?

parts.words: Material like this gives bands a chance to stretch out and play?
parts.note: rubber bands are made of stretchy stuff, while musical bands stretch out and play in a jam

explanation.surface: A music review saying the right material lets bands improvise freely.
explanation.walkthrough: The music reading of bands misleads; the bands are rubber ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Stretchy material that springs back gives rubber bands their give, hence their name.

clue.text: The way things are when one's cramming Italian

indicators.note: cramming means stuffing inside, so the Italian piece is pushed into the run before it

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
one is I and the 's stands for is, giving I'S read as IS
IT is short for Italian, as in Italian vermouth

explanation.surface: A grammar note on the state of affairs when someone studies Italian intensively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cramming' sounds like exam revision but places IT inside ASIS, between the S and the I.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means in the present condition, unchanged, describing the way things currently stand.

clue.text: Second quality diamond, say

parts.note: tone is a quality, especially of sound or colour

explanation.surface: A jeweller grading a second-rate diamond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second quality' reads as a grade of gem but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A diamond is an example of a gem, which jewellers call a precious rock; 'say' marks the example.

clue.text: Farmworker cast in drama, sweeping up yard

indicators.note: sweeping up means gathering in, so the shuffled letters take the yard letter inside
cast can mean thrown about, so the letters of in and drama are reworked

explanation.surface: A theatre scene: a farmhand cast in a play, sweeping the yard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link word but is part of the anagram, which makes DAIRMAN; the yard letter goes in after its R.
explanation.definitionFit: A dairyman works on a dairy farm milking and tending cows, so he is a farmworker.

clue.text: Submit return on capital

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to give in and the income an investment earns.

clue.text: She, say, needs to make firm declaration

parts.note: she is an example of a pronoun, the 'say' marking it as one instance
to cement something is to make it firm and fixed

explanation.surface: She has to make a firm public statement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She, say' looks like a person speaking but is an example of a part of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal public statement is a declaration, a near synonym announcing something officially.

clue.text: Long journeys — nobody miss me, guys? Just latterly!

indicators.note: just latterly means only the later half of each word is kept: the second halves of nobody, miss, me and guys

explanation.surface: A traveller setting off on long trips asks friends whether no one will miss them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just latterly' keeps the back halves: ODY, SS, E and YS.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's epic of Ulysses' wanderings gave its name to any long, eventful voyage.

clue.text: Entice mandarin mostly held in regard

indicators.note: held in means contained within, so the bird minus its tail sits inside the other word

parts.note: to regard is to see or look at

indicators.note: mostly means most of it, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: the mandarin is a species of duck

explanation.surface: A seducer holding a Chinese official in high esteem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mandarin' suggests an official or the fruit; here it is the brightly coloured duck.
explanation.definitionFit: To seduce someone is to lure or tempt them, so it is a synonym of entice.
